courses.title: .NET ML Foundations: Build and Evaluate Models with ML.NET
courses.description:
Build practical machine-learning features with C#

Learn the complete ML.NET workflow: define a prediction problem, load and transform data, train classification and regression models, evaluate them with task-appropriate metrics, save model artifacts, and serve predictions from ASP.NET Core.

The course uses code-first examples and emphasizes reproducibility, leakage prevention, operational safety, and honest measurement.
outcomes: Translate a business question into an ML.NET task, label, features, and success metric.
Load, inspect, clean, and transform data with IDataView pipelines.
Train classification and regression models and compare meaningful metrics.
Prevent target leakage and use train/test splits and cross-validation correctly.
Save, load, version, and consume ML.NET models in .NET applications.
Expose a tested prediction endpoint from ASP.NET Core.
audience: C# developers new to machine learning
Technical learners who prefer code-first ML workflows
materials: Complete C# training and inference examples
requirements: Comfort with C# classes, LINQ, and NuGet
Basic .NET console and ASP.NET Core experience

modules.title: Module 1: ML Problems, Data, and Pipelines
modules.summary: Turn a product question into a measurable ML task and create reliable ML.NET data pipelines.

lessons.title: From Product Question to ML.NET Task
lessons.content:
From Product Question to ML.NET Task

A successful ML project starts with a decision that predictions will improve. This lesson maps business questions to classification, regression, ranking, recommendation, clustering, forecasting, or anomaly-detection tasks.

Core ideas

  • Prediction target: Define exactly what the model must predict and when the answer is needed.
  • Features: Use information available at prediction time and exclude future knowledge.
  • Baseline: Compare the model with a simple rule or historical average.
  • Success metric: Choose a technical metric and a product acceptance threshold before training.

Guided implementation

  1. Create an MLContext with a fixed seed.
  2. Write input and output C# classes with clear column types.
  3. Identify the label column and the prediction-time feature boundary.
  4. Document a baseline and the cost of false positives and false negatives.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

Choose a real business scenario, write a one-page problem statement, and map it to an ML.NET task. Identify the label, five candidate features, one leakage risk, and a baseline.

Exercise checklist

  • Create a repeatable project and sample data set.
  • Implement the pipeline described in this lesson.
  • Measure the result with an appropriate metric or acceptance test.
  • Write a short note explaining one limitation and one next improvement.

Expected deliverable

A problem-definition document and a compiling console project containing the input and prediction contracts.

lessons.title: Loading, Cleaning, and Featurizing Data
lessons.content:
Loading, Cleaning, and Featurizing Data

ML.NET represents data with IDataView and composes preprocessing as estimators that become transformers after fitting. You will build one pipeline that treats data preparation as part of the model artifact.

Core ideas

  • IDataView: A lazy, schema-aware tabular abstraction that can load files, databases, or in-memory objects.
  • Schema: Column names and types form a contract between training and inference.
  • Transforms: Normalize numeric values, encode categories, featurize text, and concatenate the Features vector.
  • Missing values: Handle absence consistently instead of silently dropping unpredictable rows.

Guided implementation

  1. Load a CSV file with LoadFromTextFile and inspect a preview.
  2. Replace missing numeric values and encode a categorical column.
  3. Normalize numeric columns and concatenate all predictors into Features.
  4. Fit preprocessing only on the training partition and inspect the transformed schema.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

Prepare a small customer-churn dataset. Add missing-value handling, categorical encoding, and feature concatenation. Print five transformed rows without exposing the label as a feature.

  • Implement the pipeline described in this lesson.
  • Measure the result with an appropriate metric or acceptance test.
  • Write a short note explaining one limitation and one next improvement.

lessons.title: Classification and Regression Pipelines
lessons.content:
Classification and Regression Pipelines

This lesson builds two end-to-end pipelines and explains how the trainer must match the label and business decision. You will compare a binary classifier with a regression model and keep preprocessing attached to each trained artifact.

Core ideas

  • Binary classification: Predict one of two outcomes and return a score, probability, and predicted label.
  • Regression: Predict a continuous numeric value such as price or demand.
  • Estimator chain: Append preprocessing and trainer components before calling Fit.
  • Baseline comparison: Prefer measurable improvement over a more complicated algorithm.

Guided implementation

  1. Split the data into training and test sets.
  2. Train a binary classifier and inspect probability outputs.
  3. Train a regression pipeline on a numeric target.
  4. Save experiment parameters and compare both models with simple baselines.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

Train a sentiment classifier or churn classifier and a price regression model. Change one transform or trainer, record the metric difference, and explain whether it justifies the change.

Exercise checklist

  • Implement the pipeline described in this lesson.
  • Measure the result with an appropriate metric or acceptance test.
  • Write a short note explaining one limitation and one next improvement.

lessons.title: Metrics, Cross-Validation, and Leakage
lessons.content:
Metrics, Cross-Validation, and Leakage

An impressive metric can be meaningless when the split is wrong or the label leaks into the features. This lesson teaches metric selection, validation strategy, and diagnostic questions for suspicious results.

Core ideas

  • Classification metrics: Use precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC, PR AUC, and confusion matrices according to the decision cost.
  • Regression metrics: Use MAE, RMSE, and R-squared while inspecting error distribution.
  • Cross-validation: Estimate stability across folds when a single split is too fragile.
  • Leakage: Remove fields that reveal the outcome, including post-event timestamps or derived status values.

Guided implementation

  1. Evaluate predictions on untouched test data.
  2. Print a confusion matrix and calculate a business-relevant threshold tradeoff.
  3. Run cross-validation and compare fold variance.
  4. Perform a leakage audit and retrain after removing a suspicious feature.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

Create an intentionally leaky feature, observe the unrealistic metric, remove it, and document why the lower score is more trustworthy. Add a threshold recommendation based on business cost.

Exercise checklist

  • Create a repeatable project and sample data set.
  • Implement the pipeline described in this lesson.
  • Measure the result with an appropriate metric or acceptance test.
  • Write a short note explaining one limitation and one next improvement.

lessons.title: Saving, Loading, and Testing Model Artifacts
lessons.content:
Saving, Loading, and Testing Model Artifacts

Training and inference may run in different processes and at different times. You will preserve the transformer chain and schema, version the artifact, and create tests that detect incompatible inputs.

Core ideas

  • Model artifact: Save the trained transformer with its input schema.
  • Version metadata: Record training data window, code revision, metric, and creation time.
  • Prediction engine: Use the appropriate inference API and avoid unsafe shared mutable prediction objects.
  • Contract tests: Verify known inputs, schema compatibility, and invalid-value behavior.

Guided implementation

  1. Save the model to a versioned zip file.
  2. Load it in a separate console process.
  3. Create golden test cases with expected score ranges rather than brittle exact floats.
  4. Fail startup when the model file or expected columns are missing.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

Create a model manifest next to the zip artifact and write automated tests for two normal inputs, one boundary input, and one invalid input.

Exercise checklist

  • Create a repeatable project and sample data set.
  • Implement the pipeline described in this lesson.
  • Measure the result with an appropriate metric or acceptance test.

lessons.title: Serving Predictions with ASP.NET Core
lessons.content:
Serving Predictions with ASP.NET Core

The capstone exposes the trained model through a small ASP.NET Core API with validation, dependency injection, health checks, and observable latency.

Core ideas

  • API contract: Keep public request models separate from ML.NET training classes.
  • Concurrency: Use a safe prediction service and understand the lifetime of model objects.
  • Validation: Reject missing, impossible, or out-of-range inputs before inference.
  • Observability: Record model version, latency, errors, and aggregate score distribution without logging sensitive payloads.

Guided implementation

  1. Create a minimal API with a POST prediction endpoint.
  2. Register a singleton model loader and a safe prediction service.
  3. Add validation, structured error responses, and a model health check.
  4. Write integration tests and a small load test, then document a rollback procedure.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

courses.title: .NET Applied ML: Forecasting, Recommendations, and Anomaly Detection

Apply ML.NET to high-value business scenarios

lessons.title: Time-Series Forecasting without Future Leakage
lessons.content:
Time-Series Forecasting without Future Leakage

Forecasting requires ordered splits and a clear horizon. Random train/test splitting can leak future patterns into the past and produce misleading confidence.

Core ideas

  • Time order: Train on earlier observations and evaluate on a later holdout window.
  • Horizon: Match the number of predicted steps to the planning decision.
  • Seasonality: Represent recurring daily, weekly, or annual structure when sufficient history exists.
  • Backtesting: Repeat evaluation over several historical cutoffs to measure stability.

Guided implementation

  1. Aggregate raw events into a consistent time interval.
  2. Create a chronological training window and holdout horizon.
  3. Train an SSA forecasting pipeline and produce point forecasts with intervals.
  4. Backtest over several cutoffs and compare with a seasonal-naive baseline.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

lessons.title: Anomaly Detection and Alert Tuning
lessons.content:
Anomaly Detection and Alert Tuning

Anomaly detection identifies deviations, but an operational alert must balance sensitivity with noise. You will create spike and change-point detectors and convert raw signals into actionable incidents.

Core ideas

  • Spike: A short-lived unusual value relative to the recent pattern.
  • Change point: A sustained shift in level or behavior.
  • Sensitivity: Controls how easily the detector flags unusual observations.
  • Alert policy: Adds persistence, cooldown, suppression, and business context around model output.

Guided implementation

  1. Generate or load a signal containing normal variation, spikes, and a level shift.
  2. Run spike detection and change-point detection.
  3. Tune history length and confidence to meet an alert budget.
  4. Add consecutive-signal confirmation and a cooldown period.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

lessons.title: Recommendation Data and Matrix Factorization
lessons.content:
Recommendation Data and Matrix Factorization

Recommendation models learn latent relationships from user-item interactions. The engineering challenge begins with defining feedback and constructing a trustworthy interaction table.

Core ideas

  • Explicit feedback: Ratings or preferences directly supplied by users.
  • Implicit feedback: Clicks, views, purchases, or completion events that require weighting and negative-sample decisions.
  • Matrix factorization: Learns compact user and item factors from observed interactions.
  • Cold start: Requires fallback logic for new users and new items with little history.

Guided implementation

  1. Create indexed user and item identifiers.
  2. Convert events into a labelled interaction data set.
  3. Train a matrix-factorization model.
  4. Add popularity and category fallbacks for cold-start requests.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

lessons.title: Offline Evaluation, Bias, and Ranking Quality
lessons.content:
Offline Evaluation, Bias, and Ranking Quality

Accuracy on observed interactions does not fully describe recommendation quality. This lesson evaluates ranking, catalog coverage, novelty, and the feedback loops created by exposure.

Core ideas

  • Top-K ranking: The product consumes an ordered list, so evaluate useful items near the top.
  • Coverage: Measure how much of the catalog can be recommended.
  • Popularity bias: Frequently exposed items collect more feedback and can dominate future recommendations.
  • Evaluation split: Hold out later interactions per user to resemble the serving scenario.

Guided implementation

  1. Create a chronological per-user holdout set.
  2. Calculate precision-at-K, recall-at-K, and coverage.
  3. Compare the model with a most-popular baseline.
  4. Add a simple re-ranking rule for diversity and inspect the tradeoff.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

lessons.title: Batch and Online Inference at Scale
lessons.content:
Batch and Online Inference at Scale

Forecasts and recommendations often mix scheduled computation with request-time filtering. You will design a hybrid path that keeps latency predictable and results fresh.

Core ideas

  • Batch inference: Precompute forecasts or recommendation candidates for many entities.
  • Online inference: Score or re-rank a small candidate set using current request context.
  • Caching: Store versioned results with a freshness policy and safe fallback.
  • Throughput: Measure end-to-end capacity, allocation, and data-loading cost rather than only model execution.

Guided implementation

  1. Create a background worker that produces versioned prediction files or cache entries.
  2. Expose a low-latency query endpoint.
  3. Add cache freshness, fallback behavior, and model-version metadata.
  4. Load-test the endpoint and profile slow paths.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. lessons.title: Drift Monitoring and Safe Retraining
lessons.content:
Drift Monitoring and Safe Retraining

A production model changes only when its data or code changes, yet the world around it changes continuously. Monitoring must connect input drift, output behavior, business outcomes, and deployment history.

Core ideas

  • Data drift: Feature distributions move away from the training reference.
  • Concept drift: The relationship between features and outcomes changes.
  • Retraining trigger: Use schedules or evidence-based thresholds with minimum data requirements.
  • Promotion gate: A challenger must beat the approved baseline and pass safety checks before release.

Guided implementation

  1. Persist aggregate feature and score statistics by model version.
  2. Compare a recent window with the training reference.
  3. Run a scheduled retraining job into a candidate artifact.
  4. Evaluate, register, promote, and roll back through an explicit state machine.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

lessons.title: Chat Models through Microsoft.Extensions.AI
lessons.content:
Chat Models through Microsoft.Extensions.AI

Modern .NET applications can depend on common chat and embedding abstractions while providers remain infrastructure choices. This lesson builds a small chat service with dependency injection, middleware, and test seams.

Core ideas

  • IChatClient: Provides a common interface for chat completions and middleware composition.
  • Provider adapter: Connects the abstraction to a hosted or local model implementation.
  • Middleware: Adds logging, caching, resilience, telemetry, or policy around calls.
  • Token budget: Limits history and output so latency and cost remain controlled.

Guided implementation

  1. Create an ASP.NET Core project and register an IChatClient implementation.
  2. Add a service that accepts domain requests rather than raw provider messages.
  3. Implement timeout, retry boundaries, and cancellation.
  4. Log model, latency, token usage, and outcome without recording secrets.

lessons.title: Prompt Contracts and Structured Output
lessons.content:
Prompt Contracts and Structured Output

Natural-language output is convenient for people but fragile for software. You will define explicit instructions, schema-constrained results, validation, and recovery behavior.

Core ideas

  • Prompt contract: States the role, task, allowed evidence, output format, and refusal behavior.
  • Structured output: Maps the response to a typed schema the application can validate.
  • Few-shot examples: Demonstrate difficult boundary cases without hiding business rules in prose.
  • Recovery: Handles refusal, invalid schema, truncation, and transient failure explicitly.

Guided implementation

  1. Define a C# result type for a support-ticket triage task.
  2. Request schema-constrained output and deserialize it safely.
  3. Validate enum values, confidence, and required evidence.
  4. Create adversarial and malformed test inputs and record the expected response.

Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. lessons.title: Ingestion, Chunking, Embeddings, and Vector Storage
lessons.content:
Ingestion, Chunking, Embeddings, and Vector Storage

RAG quality begins before the chat model receives a question. The ingestion pipeline must preserve source identity, useful boundaries, metadata, and a repeatable embedding configuration.

Core ideas

  • Chunking: Split content around semantic boundaries while retaining overlap and source references.
  • Embedding: Convert text into vectors using a versioned model and known dimensions.
  • Vector data: Store vectors and filterable metadata behind a consistent .NET abstraction.
  • Idempotent ingestion: Reprocessing the same source updates records without creating duplicates.

Guided implementation

  1. Load a small set of Markdown or text documents.
  2. Create chunks with stable IDs, titles, source URLs, and section metadata.
  3. Generate embeddings and upsert records into a vector store.
  4. Track source hash, embedding model, ingestion time, and deletion state.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

lessons.title: Retrieval, Grounded Answers, and RAG Evaluation
lessons.content:
Retrieval, Grounded Answers, and RAG Evaluation

A RAG system has two systems to evaluate: retrieval must find useful evidence, and generation must answer faithfully from that evidence. You will implement citations and isolate failures.

Core ideas

  • Semantic search: Retrieves chunks similar to the query embedding.
  • Hybrid and filters: Combine semantic relevance with keywords and metadata constraints when available.
  • Grounding: Require the answer to use supplied evidence and admit when it is insufficient.
  • Evaluation set: Contains questions, expected facts, acceptable sources, and unanswerable cases.

Guided implementation

  1. Retrieve top-K chunks with metadata and optional filters.
  2. Format context with source identifiers and a strict grounding instruction.
  3. Return answer text plus citations that map to retrieved chunks.
  4. Measure retrieval hit rate, citation validity, groundedness, latency, and cost.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. Hands-on exercise

Create a 20-question evaluation set with five unanswerable questions. Tune chunk size and top-K, then compare retrieval and answer results without changing both variables at once.

  • Implement the pipeline described in this lesson.

  • Write a short note explaining one limitation and one next improvement.

A RAG endpoint, cited responses, and an evaluation table that distinguishes retrieval misses from generation errors.

modules.title: Module 3: Tools, Agents, Safety, and Delivery
modules.summary: Connect models to actions while keeping authority, verification, and production controls explicit.

lessons.title: Safe Tool Calling and Workflow Boundaries
lessons.content:
Safe Tool Calling and Workflow Boundaries

Tool calling lets a model request code execution or external actions, but application code remains responsible for authorization, validation, and side effects. This lesson designs narrow tools with auditable contracts.

Core ideas

  • Tool schema: Use precise names, descriptions, parameters, constraints, and error results.
  • Authority: The model may propose a call but cannot grant itself access or permission.
  • Confirmation boundary: Require user or policy approval immediately before consequential actions.
  • Idempotency: Use request keys and state checks to prevent duplicate side effects during retries.

Guided implementation

  1. Expose two read-only domain tools and one simulated write tool.
  2. Validate arguments and authorize each call outside the model.
  3. Add an approval state before the simulated write executes.
  4. Record correlation ID, requested arguments, approval, result, and model version.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise

Build a support assistant that can read order status and propose a refund but cannot execute the refund without an explicit approval signal. Test prompt-injection attempts inside tool data.

  • Write a short note explaining one limitation and one next improvement.

lessons.title: Agent Capstone: Evaluation, Observability, and Production Readiness
lessons.content:
Agent Capstone: Evaluation, Observability, and Production Readiness

The capstone combines chat, retrieval, and tools into a bounded assistant. The design uses an explicit workflow and stop conditions instead of relying on unlimited autonomous loops.

Core ideas

  • Agent workflow: Define states, allowed tools, stop conditions, budgets, and human handoff.
  • Evaluation: Test task success, groundedness, tool selection, argument accuracy, and unsafe-action refusal.
  • Observability: Trace model calls, retrieval, tool calls, latency, tokens, and failures with one correlation ID.
  • Defense in depth: Apply least privilege, content handling, secret isolation, rate limits, and output validation.

Guided implementation

  1. Implement a bounded assistant workflow with retrieval and two tools.
  2. Add maximum steps, time and token budgets, and a user-cancel path.
  3. Create an evaluation suite containing normal, ambiguous, adversarial, and unavailable-tool cases.
  4. Containerize the service and write deployment, rollback, and incident-response notes.

Engineering notes

Keep the data contract, transformation pipeline, and runtime behavior explicit. Record assumptions beside the code, use deterministic seeds where the API supports them, and separate experiments from production integration. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, quality threshold, and failure behavior are understood by the team that operates it.

Validate the result with data the model did not see during training. Log the model version and the important inputs needed to reproduce a prediction while avoiding secrets and personal data. Prefer a small baseline that is easy to explain before adding complexity.

Hands-on exercise
